title: Deadline-aware progressive slice-and-merge scheduler
creator: Marcus Lee
description: Problem: Current phase-splitting schedulers either bias toward low-latency single-request flow (penalizing throughput) or batch-hungry throughput that starves latency-sensitive requests. We also observe suboptimal kernel selection when slice boundaries produce small micro-batches that force fallback execution paths on some GPUs. Goal: implement a deadline-aware progressive slice-and-merge scheduler that treats each request as a (deadline, urgency) pair and dynamically splits prefill/decode work into progressive micro-slices. The scheduler merges adjacent micro-slices opportunistically to form kernel-friendly batch shapes without violating per-request deadlines. This minimizes end-to-end p95/p99 latency for latency-sensitive traffic while preserving throughput for batch-friendly workloads and maintaining fairness across tenants.
acceptance_criteria: 1) New scheduler reduces p99 latency for latency-tagged requests by >=15% under mixed workload compared to baseline scheduler, while throughput loss <=5% for throughput-tagged jobs. 2) Kernel selection telemetry shows >=20% reduction in small-fallback kernel invocations for merged slices. 3) No regressions in KV cache hit-rate or correctness. 4) Canary rollout shows stable per-tenant quotas and no higher error rates.
design_notes: Key components: (a) Deadline/urgency token embedded in request metadata (API/console tagging + inferred deadlines based on route/mode). (b) Progressive slicer that begins with a conservative prefill slice, measures actual runtime and adjusts further slice sizes. (c) Merge heuristic that considers kernel shape compatibility (seq_len, dtype/quant, attention pattern), GPU occupancy estimate, and per-request deadline slack. (d) Fairness controller that applies proportional deficit counters to avoid prolonged starvation of low-urgency requests. Kernel-awareness: merging prioritizes forming multiples of commonly-specialized kernel lengths (e.g., 128/256 tokens) to use optimized kernels. We will reuse kernel-profile metadata from kernel-probe-router (ENG-14207).
experiment_plan: Phase A (local simulator): implement progressive slicer and merge heuristic inside scheduler simulator. Run mixed workload replay (latency-tagged chat + high-throughput embedding batches) to tune merge thresholds. Phase B (staging): integrate into runtime with feature flag. Canary 10% traffic for non-critical models. Collect p50/p95/p99 token latency, small-kernel fallback counts, GPU occupancy. Phase C (production rollout): incremental ramp, evaluate for two weeks before full rollout. Metrics dashboard PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/infra-dashboards/pull/89
benchmarks: Baseline: mixed workload (60% throughput, 40% latency) staging cluster: p99 latency (latency-tagged) = 420ms; small-kernel fallback rate = 18%. Prototype (simulator tuned): p99 latency = 350ms (-16.7%), fallback rate = 12% (-33%). Throughput impact estimated -3% in simulator when merge heuristics are applied conservatively.
test_plan: Unit tests for slicer/merge logic and fairness counters. Integration tests in runtime staging that replay production traces. Load test: 48-hour mixed workload with varying request shapes and injected spikes. Kernel-selection test: assert merged batch shapes hit optimized kernels (using kernel-probe logs). Canary health checks: error rate, latency SLOs, GPU OOMs, KV cache hit-rate.
rollback_plan: Feature-flagged gate. Immediate rollback: flip feature flag if p99 latency regresses >10% or error rate increases >0.5%. Staged rollback steps documented in runbook: scale down new-scheduler nodes, route traffic back to baseline, invalidate any merge-related KV cache entries if necessary.
risks_and_mitigations: 1) Risk: Merging may increase tail latency for individual requests if merge wait time is misestimated. Mitigation: conservative time budget per-slice derived from historical latency percentiles; hedging path to break merges if deadline approaching. 2) Risk: Kernel-profile mismatch leads to worse throughput. Mitigation: use live kernel telemetry and fallback thresholds; add a learning loop to prefer merge shapes that historically succeeded. 3) Risk: fairness counters may be gamed by noisy tenants. Mitigation: apply per-tenant rate limits and anomaly detection alerts.
